articles.title: Open GPU kernel engineering series: naive GEMM to FlashAttention, H100 and Blackwell (44 sessions, code public) [P]
articles.summary: I'm building a free, code-first series on GPU kernel engineering and just published the intro and roadmap video. It's my own channel, and I'm posting to share the resource and get feedback on the plan, not to sell anything. Video: https://youtu.be/cibk7G-jHQw The core idea behind the series: for most ML workloads, kernel performance is a data-movement problem before it's a compute problem. Two things the series builds on throughout: - The roofline model. Attainable throughput is bounded by min(peak compute, memory bandwidth x arithmetic intensity), where arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved. A kernel's position relative to the ridge point tells you whether to optimize memory access or compute. - FlashAttention as the worked example. It computes exactly the same attention as the standard implementation. The gain comes from tiling so the full N x N score matrix is never written to HBM, which cuts memory traffic. We build it live. articles.summary: 🇮🇳 The Challenge: Why Generic LLMs Fail at Regulatory Compliance When an MSME manufacturer, startup founder, or laboratory engineer asks an AI: "What are the mandatory testing parameters under Scheme-I ISI Mark for IS 1786 (High Strength Deformed Steel Bars)?" Standard commercial LLMs almost always fail catastrophically. They invent fictional standard numbers, cite revoked clauses, confuse voluntary Indian Standards with mandatory Quality Control Orders (QCOs), and hallucinate chemical tolerance limits. In regulatory engineering, a single fabricated number can lead to legal penalties or factory shutdowns. articles.title: What was filling my 1 TB drive: developer and AI tools, not my files
articles.summary: My laptop has a 1 TB drive, and one day Windows told me it was nearly full. I hadn't saved anything big. So where did it all go? When I finally measured it, very little of it was "my files". Most of it was stuff developer and AI tools leave behind and never clean up: What Size on my PC Docker Desktop's disk 77 GB VirtualBox machines 36 GB Hugging Face model cache 32.5 GB Recycle Bin 18 GB npm, pip, uv, Gradle and other caches 15+ GB Why this happens Package caches (npm, pip, uv, Gradle, NuGet, Cargo...) keep every version you ever downloaded. They are safe to clear: the tool downloads again what it needs. AI models from Ollama, LM Studio and Hugging Face are several GB each. It's easy to try five models and forget four of them. Docker and WSL disks (.vhdx files) grow but never shrink by themselves, even after you delete images or files inside them.
